{{refimprove|date=November 2013}}
{{no footnotes|date=May 2024}}
In [[mathematics]], and more specifically in [[numerical analysis]], '''Householder's methods''' are a class of [[root-finding algorithm]]s that are used for functions of one real variable with continuous derivatives up to some order {{math|''d'' + 1}}. Each of these methods is characterized by the number {{mvar|d}}, which is known as the ''order'' of the method. The algorithm is iterative and has an [[order of convergence]] of {{math|''d'' + 1}}.

These methods are named after the American mathematician [[Alston Scott Householder]]. The case of {{math|1=''d'' = 1}} corresponds to [[Newton's method]]; the case of {{math|1=''d'' = 2}} corresponds to [[Halley's method]].

== Method ==

Householder's method is a numerical algorithm for solving the equation {{math|1=''f''(''x'') = 0}}. In this case, the function {{mvar|f}} has to be a function of one real variable. The method{{sfn|Householder|1970|p=[https://archive.org/details/numericaltreatme0000hous/page/169 169]}} consists of a sequence of iterations

<math display=block>x_{n+1} = x_n + d\; \frac {\left(1/f\right)^{(d-1)}(x_n)} {\left(1/f\right)^{(d)}(x_n)} </math>

beginning with an initial guess {{math|''x''<sub>0</sub>}}, where the superscript in parentheses indicates the number of times the function is [[derivative|differentiated]].

If {{mvar|f}} is a {{math|''d'' + 1}} times continuously [[differentiable function]] and {{mvar|a}} is a zero of {{mvar|f}} but not of its derivative, then, in a neighborhood of {{mvar|a}}, the iterates {{math|''x''<sub>''n''</sub>}} satisfy:{{cn|date=May 2018}}

<math display=block>| x_{n+1} - a | \le K \cdot {| x_n - a |}^{d+1},</math>
for some <math>K > 0.</math>

This means that the iterates converge to the zero if the initial guess is sufficiently close, and that the convergence has order {{math|''d'' + 1}} or better.  Furthermore, when close enough to {{mvar|a}}, it commonly is the case that <math>x_{n+1} - a \approx C (x_n - a)^{d+1}</math> for some <math>C \ne 0</math>.  In particular,
* if {{mvar|d}} is odd and {{math|''C'' > 0}} then convergence to {{mvar|a}} will be from values greater than {{mvar|a}};
* if {{mvar|d}} is odd and {{math|''C'' < 0}} then convergence to {{mvar|a}} will be from values less than {{mvar|a}};
* if {{mvar|d}} is even and {{math|''C'' > 0}} then convergence to {{mvar|a}} will be from the side where it starts; and
* if {{mvar|d}} is even and {{math|''C'' < 0}} then convergence to {{mvar|a}} will alternate sides.

Despite their order of convergence, these methods are not widely used when {{math|''d'' ≥ 3}} because the gain in precision is not commensurate with the rise in effort. The ''Ostrowski index'' expresses the error reduction in the number of function evaluations instead of the iteration count.{{sfn|Ostrowski|1966}}
* For polynomials, the evaluation of the first {{mvar|d}} derivatives of {{mvar|f}} at {{math|''x''<sub>''n''</sub>}} using [[Horner's method]] has an effort of {{math|''d'' + 1}} polynomial evaluations. Since {{math|''n''(''d'' + 1)}} evaluations over {{mvar|n}} iterations give an [[error exponent]] of {{math|(''d'' + 1)<sup>''n''</sup>}}, the exponent for one function evaluation is <math>\sqrt[d+1]{d+1}</math>, numerically {{math|1.4142}}, {{math|1.4422}}, {{math|1.4142}}, {{math|1.3797}} for {{math|1=''d'' = 1, 2, 3, 4}}, and falling after that.  By this criterion, the {{math|1=''d'' = 2}} case ([[Halley's method]]) is the optimal value of {{mvar|d}}.
* For general functions the derivative evaluation using the Taylor arithmetic of [[automatic differentiation]] requires the equivalent of {{math|(''d'' + 1)(''d'' + 2)/2}} function evaluations. One function evaluation thus reduces the error by an exponent of <math>\sqrt[\frac{(d+1)(d+2)}{2}]{d+1}</math>, which is <math>\sqrt[3]{2}\approx 1.2599</math> for Newton's method, <math>\sqrt[6]{3}\approx 1.2009</math> for Halley's method and falling towards 1 or linear convergence for the higher order methods.

== Motivation ==

=== First approach ===

Suppose {{mvar|f}} is analytic in a neighborhood of {{mvar|a}} and {{math|1=''f''(''a'') = 0}}.  Then {{mvar|f}} has a [[Taylor series]] at {{mvar|a}} and its [[constant term]] is zero.  Because this constant term is zero, the function {{math|''f''(''x'') / (''x'' − ''a'')}} will have a Taylor series at {{mvar|a}} and, when {{math|1=''f ′'' (''a'') ≠ 0}}, its constant term will not be zero.  Because that constant term is not zero, it follows that the reciprocal {{math|(''x'' − ''a'') / ''f''(''x'')}} has a Taylor series at {{mvar|a}}, which we will write as <math>\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{c_k (x-a)^k}{k!}</math> and its constant term {{math|''c''{{sub|0}}}} will not be zero.  Using that Taylor series we can write
<math display=block>\frac{1}{f} = \frac{c_{0}}{x-a} + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{c_{k} (x-a)^{k-1}}{k~(k-1)!}\,.</math>
When we compute its {{mvar|d}}-th derivative, we note that the terms for {{math|1=''k'' = 1, ..., ''d''}} conveniently vanish:
<math display=block>\left(\frac{1}{f}\right)^{(d)}
= \frac{(-1)^d d!~c_{0}}{(x-a)^{d+1}} + \sum_{k=d+1}^{\infty} \frac{c_{k} (x-a)^{k-d-1}}{k~(k-d-1)!}</math>
<math display=block>= \frac{(-1)^d d!~c_{0}}{(x-a)^{d+1}} \left(1 + \frac{1}{(-1)^d d!~c_{0}}\sum_{k=d+1}^{\infty} \frac{c_{k} (x-a)^{k}}{k~(k-d-1)!}\right)</math>
<math display=block>= \frac{(-1)^d d!~c_{0}}{(x-a)^{d+1}} \left(1 + \mathcal{O}\left((x-a)^{d+1}\right)\right)
\,,</math>
using [[big O notation]].  We thus get that the correction term that we add to {{math|1=''x'' = ''x''{{sub|''n''}}}} to get a value of {{math|''x''{{sub|''n''+1}}}} that is closer to {{mvar|a}} is:
<math display=block>d~\frac{(1/f)^{(d-1)}}{(1/f)^{(d)}}
= d~\frac{(-1)^{d-1} (d-1)!~c_{0}}{(-1)^d d!~c_{0}} (x-a) \left( \frac{1 + \mathcal{O}\left((x-a)^{d}\right)}{1 + \mathcal{O}\left((x-a)^{d+1}\right)} \right)</math>
<math display=block>= -\left( (x-a) + \mathcal{O}\left((x-a)^{d+1}\right) \right)\,.</math>
Thus, <math> x + d~\frac{(1/f)^{(d-1)}}{(1/f)^{(d)}}</math> is {{tmath|a + \mathcal{O}\left((x-a)^{d+1}\right)}}.

=== Second approach ===

Suppose {{math|1=''x'' = ''a''}} is a simple root. Then near {{math|1=''x'' = ''a''}}, {{math|(1/''f'')(''x'')}} is a [[meromorphic function]]. Suppose we have the [[Taylor expansion]]:
<math display=block>
(1/f)(x) = \sum_{d=0}^{\infty} \frac{(1/f)^{(d)}(b)}{d!} (x-b)^d
</math>
around a point {{mvar|b}} that is closer to {{mvar|a}} than it is to any other zero of {{mvar|f}}.  By [[König's theorem (complex analysis)|König's theorem]], we have:
<math display=block>
a-b = \lim_{d\rightarrow \infty} \frac{\frac{(1/f)^{(d-1)}(b)}{(d-1)!}}{\frac{(1/f)^{(d)}(b)}{d!}}=\lim_{d\rightarrow \infty} d\frac{(1/f)^{(d-1)}(b)}{(1/f)^{(d)}(b)}.
</math>

This suggests that Householder's iteration might be a good convergent iteration. The actual proof of the convergence is also based on these ideas.

== The methods of lower order ==

Householder's method of order 1 is just [[Newton's method]], since:
<math display=block>\begin{array}{rl}
x_{n+1} =& x_n + 1\,\frac {\left(1/f\right)(x_n)} {\left(1/f\right)^{(1)}(x_n)}\\[.7em]
=& x_n + \frac{1}{f(x_n)}\cdot\left(\frac{-f'(x_n)}{f(x_n)^2}\right)^{-1}\\[.7em]
=& x_n - \frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}.
\end{array}
</math>

For Householder's method of order 2 one gets [[Halley's method]], since the identities
<math display=block>\textstyle 
  (1/f)'(x)=-\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)^2}\ 
</math>
and
<math display=block>\textstyle\ 
  (1/f)''(x)=-\frac{f''(x)}{f(x)^2}+2\frac{f'(x)^2}{f(x)^3}</math>
result in
<math display=block>\begin{array}{rl}
x_{n+1} =& x_n + 2\,\frac {\left(1/f\right)'(x_n)} {\left(1/f\right)''(x_n)}\\[1em]
=& x_n + \frac{-2f(x_n)\,f'(x_n)}{-f(x_n)f''(x_n)+2f'(x_n)^2}\\[1em]
=& x_n - \frac{f(x_n)f'(x_n)}{f'(x_n)^2-\tfrac12f(x_n)f''(x_n)}\\[1em]
=& x_n + h_n\;\frac{1}{1+\frac12(f''/f')(x_n)\,h_n}.
\end{array}
</math>
In the last line, <math>h_n=-\tfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}</math> is the update of the Newton iteration at the point <math>x_n</math>. This line was added to demonstrate where the difference to the simple Newton's method lies.

The third order method is obtained from the identity of the third order derivative of {{math|1/''f''}}
<math display=block>\textstyle
  (1/f)'''(x)=-\frac{f'''(x)}{f(x)^2}+6\frac{f'(x)\,f''(x)}{f(x)^3}-6\frac{f'(x)^3}{f(x)^4}
</math>
and has the formula
<math display=block>\begin{array}{rl}
x_{n+1} =& x_n + 3\,\frac {\left(1/f\right)''(x_n)} {\left(1/f\right)'''(x_n)}\\[1em]
=& x_n - \frac{6f(x_n)\,f'(x_n)^2-3f(x_n)^2f''(x_n)}{6f'(x_n)^3-6f(x_n)f'(x_n)\,f''(x_n)+f(x_n)^2\,f'''(x_n)}\\[1em]
=& x_n + h_n\frac{1+\frac12(f''/f')(x_n)\,h_n}{1+(f''/f')(x_n)\,h_n+\frac16(f'''/f')(x_n)\,h_n^2}
\end{array}
</math>
and so on.

== Example ==
The first problem solved by Newton with the Newton-Raphson-Simpson method was the polynomial equation <math>y^3-2y-5=0</math>. He observed that there should be a solution close to 2. Replacing {{math|1=''y'' = ''x'' + 2}} transforms the equation into
<math display=block>0=f(x)=-1 + 10 x + 6 x^2 + x^3</math>.
The Taylor series of the reciprocal function starts with
<math display=block>\begin{array}{rl}
1/f(x)=& - 1 - 10\,x - 106 \,x^2 - 1121 \,x^3 - 11856 \,x^4 - 125392 \,x^5\\
       & - 1326177 \,x^6 - 14025978 \,x^7 - 148342234 \,x^8 - 1568904385 \,x^9\\
       & - 16593123232 \,x^{10} +O(x^{11})
\end{array}</math>
The result of applying Householder's methods of various orders at {{math|1=''x'' = 0}} is also obtained by dividing neighboring coefficients of the latter [[power series]]. For the first orders one gets the following values after just one iteration step: For an example, in the case of the 3rd order,
<math> x_1 = 0.0 + 106/1121 = 0.09455842997324</math>.

== Derivation ==

An exact derivation of Householder's methods starts from the [[Padé approximation]] of order {{math|''d'' + 1}} of the function, where the approximant with linear [[numerator]] is chosen. Once this has been achieved, the update for the next approximation results from computing the unique zero of the numerator.

The Padé approximation has the form
<math display=block>f(x+h)=\frac{a_0+h}{b_0+b_1h+\cdots+b_{d-1}h^{d-1}}+O(h^{d+1}).</math>
The [[rational function]] has a zero at <math>h=-a_0</math>.

Just as the Taylor polynomial of degree {{mvar|d}} has {{math|''d'' + 1}} coefficients that depend on the function {{mvar|f}}, the Padé approximation also has {{math|''d'' + 1}} coefficients dependent on {{mvar|f}} and its derivatives. More precisely, in any Padé approximant, the degrees of the numerator and denominator polynomials have to add to the order of the approximant. Therefore, <math>b_d=0</math> has to hold.

One could determine the Padé approximant starting from the Taylor polynomial of {{mvar|f}} using [[Euclid's algorithm]]. However, starting from the Taylor polynomial of {{math|1/''f''}} is shorter and leads directly to the given formula. Since
<math display=block>
  (1/f)(x+h) = 
     (1/f)(x)+(1/f)'(x)h+\cdots+(1/f)^{(d-1)}(x)\frac{h^{d-1}}{(d-1)!}+(1/f)^{(d)}(x)\frac{h^d}{d!}+O(h^{d+1})
</math>
has to be equal to the inverse of the desired rational function, we get after multiplying with <math>a_0+h</math> in the power <math>h^d</math> the equation
<math display=block>0=b_d=a_0(1/f)^{(d)}(x)\frac1{d!}+(1/f)^{(d-1)}(x)\frac1{(d-1)!}</math>.

Now, solving the last equation for the zero <math>h=-a_0</math> of the numerator results in
<math display=block>\begin{align}
  h&=-a_0=
    \frac{\frac1{(d-1)!}(1/f)^{(d-1)}(x)}{\frac1{d!}(1/f)^{(d)}(x)}\\
  &=d\,\frac{(1/f)^{(d-1)}(x)}{(1/f)^{(d)}(x)}
\end{align}</math>.

This implies the iteration formula
<math display=block>x_{n+1} = x_n + d\; \frac { \left(1/f\right)^{(d-1)} (x_n) } { \left(1/f\right)^{(d)} (x_n) } </math>.

== Relation to Newton's method ==
Householder's method applied to the real-valued function {{math|''f''(''x'')}} is the same as applying Newton's method
<math display=block>x_{n+1} = x_n - \frac{g(x_n)}{g'(x_n)}</math>
to find the zeros of the function:
<math display=block>g(x) = \left|(1/f)^{(d-1)}\right|^{-1/d}\,,</math>
where we are computing a {{math|(''d'' − 1)}}-th derivative and raising to a power of {{math|−1/''d''}}.
In particular, {{math|1=''d'' = 1}} gives Newton's method unmodified and {{math|1=''d'' = 2}} gives Halley's method.
